title: “Doubt is our product”: the template
body: An internal Brown & Williamson tobacco memo, quoted by a federal judge in 2006, says: “Doubt is our product since it is the best means of competing with the ‘body of fact’ that exists in the mind of the general public.” A 2007 Union of Concerned Scientists report found ExxonMobil drew on the same tactics, and some of the same groups, to cast doubt on climate science.
src_label: US v. Philip Morris, Amended Final Opinion (D.D.C. 2006); Union of Concerned Scientists (2007)

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (hosted by the U.S. Department of Justice)
sources.title: United States v. Philip Morris USA, Inc., Civil Action No. 99-2496 (GK), Amended Final Opinion
quotes: At the same time, an internal B&W document titled "Smoking and Health Proposal" explained: "Doubt is our product since it is the best means of competing with the 'body of fact' that exists in the mind of the general public. It is also a means of establishing a controversy." 690010951-0959 at 0954 (US 21040).

sources.title: Smoke, Mirrors & Hot Air: How ExxonMobil Uses Big Tobacco's Tactics to Manufacture Uncertainty on Climate Science
quotes: As one famous internal memo from the Brown & Williamson tobacco company put it: “Doubt is our product, since it is the best means of competing with the ‘body of fact’ that exists in the minds of the general public. It is also the means of establishing a controversy.”
Brown & Williamson (B&W), 1969, Smoking and health proposal
ExxonMobil has drawn upon the tactics and even some of the organizations and actors involved in the callous disinformation campaign the tobacco industry waged for 40 years.

changes: Quoted the memo exactly instead of paraphrasing it, and named who documented the climate link (UCS). Replaced the SourceWatch URL with the federal court opinion that quotes the memo and the UCS report.
notes: The court quotes the memo twice. In one place it calls it 'an undated internal B&W document' and gives slightly different wording ('It is also the means of...'). The 1969 date comes from UCS, which cites the same Bates range (690010951-0959). The memo's 'body of fact' is what the public believed about smoking and health. It does not literally say 'linking smoking to cancer', so the body now quotes it.

title: Oil company “advertorials” on the opinion page
body: Mobil (later ExxonMobil) bought an advertorial on the New York Times op-ed page every Thursday from 1972 to 2001. A peer-reviewed analysis found 81% of its climate advertorials expressed doubt, while 80% of its internal documents and 83% of its peer-reviewed papers acknowledged that climate change is real and human-caused.
src_label: Supran & Oreskes, Environmental Research Letters (Aug 2017)

sources.title: Assessing ExxonMobil's climate change communications (1977–2014), Supran & Oreskes, Environ. Res. Lett. 12 084019
quotes: For example, accounting for expressions of reasonable doubt, 83% of peer-reviewed papers and 80% of internal documents acknowledge that climate change is real and human-caused, yet only 12% of advertorials do so, with 81% instead expressing doubt.
The company took out an advertorial every Thursday between 1972 and 2001 [29].
bought one-quarter of all advertorials on the Op-Ed page
36 Mobil/ExxonMobil advertorials related to climate change in the NYT
of the 72% (26/36) of climate change advertorials that take a position, 81% (21/26) take the position of ‘Doubt’

changes: Start year 1970 -> 1972: the paper says the weekly advertorials ran 'every Thursday between 1972 and 2001'. Changed 'its scientists' papers' to 'its peer-reviewed papers', the paper's term, and dropped 'about' from the 80%. Year label 1970– -> 1972–2004, because the climate advertorials analysed run 1989–2004.
notes: IOP's site sits behind a bot check (Radware captcha), so I did not read it directly. I checked the text against the CC-BY PDF of the same article mirrored at reteclima.it, and checked the 'every Thursday' sentence against the IOP HTML through a fetch. In the PDF that sentence is split by footnote 3. The 81% is the share of the 26 position-taking advertorials (21/26); the sample is 36 climate advertorials, 1989–2004.

title: False balance in the prestige press
body: A study of global-warming coverage in the New York Times, Washington Post, Los Angeles Times and Wall Street Journal from 1988 to 2002 found that most articles (52.65%) gave “roughly equal attention” to the view that humans were warming the planet and the view that natural fluctuations could explain it. The authors concluded this “balance” was itself a bias that pulled public discussion away from the science.
src_label: Boykoff & Boykoff, “Balance as bias,” Global Environmental Change (2004)

sources.publisher: Global Environmental Change 14 (2004) 125–136 (PDF hosted by the University of Colorado Center for Science and Technology Policy Research)
sources.title: Balance as bias: global warming and the US prestige press, Maxwell T. Boykoff and Jules M. Boykoff
quotes: This paper demonstrates that US prestige-press coverage of global warming from 1988 to 2002 has contributed to a significant divergence of popular discourse from scientific discourse.

Through content analysis of US prestige press— meaning the New York Times, the Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, and the Wall Street Journal—this paper focuses on the norm of balanced reporting, and shows that the prestige press's adherence to balance actually leads to biased coverage of both anthropogenic contributions to global warming and resultant action.

We found that in the majority (52.65%) of coverage in the US prestige press, balanced accounts prevailed; these accounts gave ‘‘roughly equal attention’’ to the view that humans were contributing to global warming, and the other view that exclusively natural fluctuations could explain the earth's temperature increase.
Our sample contained 636 articles, which is 18.4% of the population.

changes: Added the study's figure (52.65%) and quoted its definition of 'balanced'. Replaced the MediaWell (SSRC) citation page with the paper itself.
notes: The 52.65% is of the 340 sampled articles that addressed whether humans contribute to warming (Fig. 1, n = 340); the full random sample was 636 of 3,543 articles. The PDF is the publisher's typeset version ('ARTICLE IN PRESS'), hosted at the University of Colorado. The DOI is 10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2003.10.001.

title: Enron, “America’s Most Innovative Company”
body: Fortune magazine named Enron “America’s Most Innovative Company” six years running, a line Enron was still printing on its press releases in August 2001, months before it went bankrupt. The SEC later charged its chairman, Kenneth Lay, with a scheme to defraud that included falsifying its reported financial results.

sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Enron Task Force trial exhibits (Government Exhibit 959, Crim. No. H-04-25)
sources.title: Enron news release: Enron Announces Skilling Resignation; Lay Assumes President and CEO Duties
quotes: Fortune magazine has named Enron "America's Most Innovative Company" for six consecutive years.
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: Tuesday, August 14, 2001

sources.title: SEC Charges Kenneth L. Lay, Enron's Former Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, with Fraud and Insider Trading
quotes: The Securities and Exchange Commission today initiated civil charges against Kenneth L. Lay, former Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Enron Corp., for his role in a wide-ranging scheme to defraud by falsifying Enron's publicly reported financial results and making false and misleading public representations about Enron's business performance and financial condition.
did not learn of Lay's sales of Enron stock back to the company until February 2002, over two months after Enron filed for bankruptcy protection.

changes: No factual change. Added URLs: Enron's own boilerplate, as entered in evidence by the Justice Department, and the SEC's fraud charges against Lay. Slightly reworded so each claim maps to a source.
notes: I did not read Fortune's own rankings archive. The 'six consecutive years' claim is Enron's, as printed on its August 2001 release. Read with the 2001 ranking, that gives 1996–2001. The source is the DOJ's OCR text of the exhibit, so the quotes are OCR text, which here reads cleanly.

title: “Bear Stearns is fine!”
body: On March 11, 2008, CNBC’s Jim Cramer answered a viewer asking whether to pull his money out of Bear Stearns: “No, no, no. Bear Stearns is fine. Do not take your money… Don’t move your money from Bear.” Five days later JPMorgan agreed to buy the bank for about $2 a share, later raised to about $10. Cramer said afterwards he had meant money held at Bear, not its stock.
src_label: CNBC Mad Money transcript via Columbia Journalism Review (Mar 2008); JPMorgan Chase releases filed with the SEC (Mar 16 & 24, 2008)

sources.publisher: Columbia Journalism Review (Dean Starkman, The Audit)
sources.title: In the Mad Money Swamp
quotes: Peter writes: Should I be worried about Bear Stearns in terms of liquidity and get my money out of there? No, no, no. Bear Stearns is fine. Do not take your money…if there's one take away other than (unintelligible) … Bear Stearns is not in trouble. It's more likely to be taken over. Don't move your money from Bear. That's just being silly. Don't be silly.
The questioner was an e-mail, directly asked whether his money was safe at bear Stearns. He did not ask me about Bear Stearns stock.

sources.publisher: JPMorgan Chase & Co., Form 8-K exhibit (SEC EDGAR)
sources.title: JPMorgan Chase To Acquire Bear Stearns
quotes: New York, March 16, 2008 -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM) announced it is acquiring The Bear Stearns Companies Inc. (NYSE: BSC).
Based on the closing price of March 15, 2008, the transaction would have a value of approximately $2 per share.

sources.publisher: JPMorgan Chase & Co., Form 8-K exhibit (SEC EDGAR)
sources.title: JPMorgan Chase and Bear Stearns Announce Amended Merger Agreement
quotes: reflecting an implied value of approximately $10 per share of Bear Stearns common stock based on the closing price of JPMorgan Chase common stock on the New York Stock Exchange on March 20, 2008.

sources.title: Should You Stay Away From Jim Cramer?
quotes: Cramer and CNBC have defended his statements, arguing that Cramer's assertions on the bank were in reference to a viewer's question on Bear Stearns' liquidity, not its stock prices.

changes: Replaced the composite quote ('Bear Stearns is fine! Do not move your money from Bear.') with the words as transcribed. 'Sold for $2 a share' -> 'agreed to buy for about $2 a share, later raised to about $10': the $2 was the first offer, and JPMorgan raised it on March 24. Dropped 'a fraction of its value', which none of these sources states as such. Added Cramer's defence (he meant money held at Bear), which CNBC and ABC report.
notes: CJR prints the transcript excerpt inside a sarcastic column, but the quoted words are the broadcast's. ABC prints a shorter version ('Don't move your money from Bear! That's just being silly! Don't be silly!'). If a value comparison is wanted, CJR says the shares 'crashed from $35 to $2' within days, and Cramer himself said Bear was 'then trading at $35' on Friday, March 14.

title: Celebrity crypto promotions
body: Kim Kardashian paid $1.26 million to settle SEC charges that she promoted EthereumMax’s EMAX token on Instagram without disclosing that she was paid $250,000 for the post. FTX, one of the biggest advertisers in the 2022 Super Bowl, was bankrupt within 10 months.
src_label: SEC press release (Oct 3, 2022); Associated Press (Feb 2023)

sources.title: SEC Charges Kim Kardashian for Unlawfully Touting Crypto Security
quotes: The Securities and Exchange Commission today announced charges against Kim Kardashian for touting on social media a crypto asset security offered and sold by EthereumMax without disclosing the payment she received for the promotion. Kardashian agreed to settle the charges, pay $1.26 million in penalties, disgorgement, and interest, and cooperate with the Commission's ongoing investigation.

The SEC's order finds that Kardashian failed to disclose that she was paid $250,000 to publish a post on her Instagram account about EMAX tokens, the crypto asset security being offered by EthereumMax.

sources.publisher: Associated Press (Ken Sweet and Mae Anderson), as syndicated by KSAT
sources.title: Year after 'Crypto Bowl,' crypto ads vanish from big game
quotes: Cryptocurrency exchange FTX was one of biggest advertisers in last year's Super Bowl, featuring ads that included celebrity comedian Larry David.
Within 10 months of the Super Bowl, FTX was bankrupt.
The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection on November 11.

changes: No factual change. Added the token's name, the $250,000 payment and 'within 10 months' from the sources, and added URLs.
notes: The FTX sentence rests on AP reporting, not on a ruling. The 'court' tag fits the Kardashian half (an SEC settled order). Kardashian settled without admitting or denying the findings. I read the AP story on a syndicating station's site because apnews.com was not fetched; the byline and text are AP's.

title: Facebook secretly manipulates users’ moods
body: For one week in January 2012, Facebook altered the News Feeds of 689,003 users to test whether emotions spread: those shown fewer positive posts wrote fewer positive posts and more negative ones. The only consent was Facebook’s general Data Use Policy, and the journal that published the study issued an “expression of concern” about informed consent.
src_label: Kramer, Guillory & Hancock, PNAS (June 2014); PNAS Editorial Expression of Concern (July 2014)

sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PubMed Central copy)
sources.title: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks, Kramer, Guillory & Hancock, PNAS 111(24):8788–8790, doi:10.1073/pnas.1320040111
quotes: The experiment manipulated the extent to which people (N = 689,003) were exposed to emotional expressions in their News Feed.
The experiments took place for 1 wk (January 11–18, 2012).
When positive expressions were reduced, people produced fewer positive posts and more negative posts; when negative expressions were reduced, the opposite pattern occurred.
As such, it was consistent with Facebook's Data Use Policy, to which all users agree prior to creating an account on Facebook, constituting informed consent for this research.

sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Inder M. Verma, Editor-in-Chief)
sources.title: Editorial Expression of Concern: Experimental evidence of massive-scale emotional contagion through social networks, PNAS 111(29):10779
quotes: Questions have been raised about the principles of informed consent and opportunity to opt out in connection with the research in this paper.

It is nevertheless a matter of concern that the collection of the data by Facebook may have involved practices that were not fully consistent with the principles of obtaining informed consent and allowing participants to opt out.

changes: 'About 689,000' -> 689,003, with the dates (Jan 11–18, 2012). 'Without their knowledge' -> what the record shows: the only consent was the Data Use Policy, and PNAS published an expression of concern. Neither source says users were told nothing in so many words. 'Happier or sadder' -> what was measured, which was users' own posts. Added URLs.
notes: pnas.org is behind a Cloudflare check. I read the expression of concern from a Wayback Machine capture of its original PNAS URL. The paper itself is on PubMed Central. The title word 'secretly' is fair given the consent finding, but the editor may prefer 'quietly'.

title: Cambridge Analytica
body: Facebook data on up to 87 million people, by Facebook’s own estimate, reached the data firm Cambridge Analytica, which the FTC says used it for voter profiling and targeted advertising. The FTC fined Facebook a record $5 billion for deceiving users about their ability to control their privacy.
src_label: FTC press releases (July 24, 2019); Facebook newsroom (Apr 4, 2018)

sources.title: FTC Imposes $5 Billion Penalty and Sweeping New Privacy Restrictions on Facebook
quotes: Facebook, Inc. will pay a record-breaking $5 billion penalty, and submit to new restrictions and a modified corporate structure that will hold the company accountable for the decisions it makes about its users' privacy, to settle Federal Trade Commission charges that the company violated a 2012 FTC order by deceiving users about their ability to control the privacy of their personal information.

sources.title: FTC Sues Cambridge Analytica, Settles with Former CEO and App Developer
quotes: alleging they employed deceptive tactics to harvest personal information from tens of millions of Facebook users for voter profiling and targeting.

Cambridge Analytica, Kogan, and Nix then matched these personality scores with U.S. voter records. The company used these matched personality scores for its voter profiling and targeted advertising services.
as well as 50 million to 65 million of those users' Facebook friends, including at least 30 million identifiable U.S. consumers.

sources.publisher: Facebook (Meta) Newsroom, Mike Schroepfer, Chief Technology Officer
sources.title: An Update on Our Plans to Restrict Data Access on Facebook
quotes: In total, we believe the Facebook information of up to 87 million people — mostly in the US — may have been improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica.

changes: No factual change. Said where the 87 million comes from (Facebook), quoted the FTC's description of the voter targeting, and added URLs.
notes: The $5 billion settled Facebook's violation of its 2012 FTC order. The Cambridge Analytica sharing was one part of a wider privacy case, not the only basis. The FTC's own count is 50–65 million friends plus 250,000–270,000 app users. 'Up to 87 million' is Facebook's figure. ftc.gov blocks scripted fetches, so I read the two FTC releases in a browser and copied the quotes from the page text.

title: Sinclair’s must-run scripts
body: Sinclair Broadcast Group, which owned more than 190 local TV stations, more than any other company, had its anchors read an identical script warning about “biased and false news.” A 98-second Deadspin montage of dozens of them reciting it went viral.
src_label: NPR (Apr 2, 2018); NBC News (Apr 2, 2018)

sources.title: Video Reveals Power Of Sinclair, As Local News Anchors Recite Script In Unison
quotes: A video published by sports news site Deadspin over the weekend revealed dozens of TV anchors from Sinclair Broadcast Group reciting the same speech warning against "biased and false news."
Sinclair owns more than 190 TV stations across the country, more than any other media company, and is seeking to acquire dozens more by purchasing Tribune Media.
The company recently began instructing local anchors to read a script denouncing "fake" news.

sources.title: TV anchors decrying "fake" news put spotlight on Sinclair
quotes: In March, TV anchors at broadcast stations across the U.S. began reading from an identical script passed down to them by their owner — Sinclair Broadcast Group.
But the segments didn't receive widespread attention until Saturday, when the website Deadspin published a 98-second video montage of the TV segments that went viral.

changes: No factual change. Added the station count, the script's words and the montage's length from the sources, and added NPR.
notes: The 'documented' tag rests on the broadcasts themselves, which are public. The sources here are news reports. NBC notes that it 'was not immediately clear how many Sinclair stations aired a version of the script'. 'Dozens' is what the montage showed.

title: The CIA and the press
body: The Senate’s Church Committee reported in 1976 that about 50 of the CIA’s assets were American journalists or employees of US media organizations, and that about half of these relationships were paid.
src_label: Church Committee final report, Book I: Foreign and Military Intelligence (1976), pp. 195, 455

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities (Church Committee), Report No. 94-755
sources.title: Final Report, Book I: Foreign and Military Intelligence
quotes: About half of the some 50 CIA relationships with the U.S. media were paid relationships

changes: No factual change. Added that about half the relationships were paid (p. 195). Replaced the CIA reading-room link: that document ID now redirects to the reading room's home page.
notes: The Senate's PDF is a scan with no text layer. I checked the quotes against the OCR text of the same report on the Internet Archive (identifier pdfy-UM4X5C4pdvn8FqLd). The 'approximately 50' sentence is on p. 455; the 'paid relationships' sentence is on p. 195. The CIA's own copy is in its reading room as CIA-RDP05S00620R000601470021-1. The count is as of the CIA's February 11, 1976 announcement of new media guidelines.

t: false statements about Iraq’s threat by President Bush and seven top officials in the two years after 9/11, by one count.
src_label: Center for Public Integrity, “False Pretenses” (Jan 2008)

sources.title: False Pretenses

Bush and seven of his administration's top officials, including Vice President Dick Cheney, National Security Adviser Condoleezza Rice, and Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld, made at least 935 false statements in the two years following September 11, 2001, about the national security threat posed by Saddam Hussein's Iraq.
