sources.title: New report shows more than $1B from war industry and govt. going to top 50 think tanks
quotes: A report released today from the Foreign Influence Transparency Initiative, or FITI, at the Center for International Policy, where I work, reveals more than $1 billion in defense contractor and U.S. government funds flowing to the top 50 most influential U.S. think tanks from 2014-2019.

sources.publisher: Center for International Policy report pages (DocumentCloud copy)
sources.title: U.S. Government and Defense Contractor Funding of America's Top 50 Think Tanks (excerpt)
quotes: This analysis identified more than $1.078 billion in U.S. government and defense contractor funding going to the top 50 think tanks in America.
raking in a whopping $1.029 billion between 2014-2019

sources.title: Top 50 U.S. Think Tanks Receive Over $1B from Gov, Defense Contractors
quotes: The RAND Corporation alone received over $1 billion between 2014-2019, accounting for approximately 95 percent of its funding that the report tracked.

changes: No factual change. Replaced 'most of it' with the report's figure, about 95% ($1.029 billion), and noted that RAND's money came almost entirely from government sources rather than contractors.
notes: The DocumentCloud copy is a scan of report pages. I read it from a Wayback Machine capture, because DocumentCloud blocked direct access, and its OCR has small errors, so only clean phrases are quoted. That copy's table prints RAND as $1,209,100,000, but its text and TAC give $1.029 billion, so the table is a typo. The report itself says the totals are minimums. Worth knowing for the framing: RAND's share was nearly all from DoD, the Air Force, the Army and DHS, so the 'defense contractor' money to the other 49 think tanks is a few tens of millions.

title: The Senate investigates the “merchants of death”
body: The Senate’s Nye Committee held 93 hearings on the munitions industry and the economic circumstances of US entry into World War I, questioning J. P. Morgan Jr. and Pierre du Pont. It found little hard evidence of a conspiracy to drag the country into war, but reported that arms makers opposed almost every disarmament proposal, profited when they failed, and that national defense had not been kept separate from their lobbying.
src_label: U.S. Senate Historical Office; Senate Report No. 944, Special Committee Investigating the Munitions Industry (1936)

sources.title: "Merchants of Death"
quotes: The so-called Senate Munitions Committee came into being because of widespread reports that manufacturers of armaments had unduly influenced the American decision to enter the war in 1917. These weapons suppliers had reaped enormous profits at the cost of more than 53,000 American battle deaths.

Over the next 18 months, the Nye Committee held 93 hearings, questioning more than 200 witnesses, including J. P. Morgan, Jr., and Pierre du Pont. Committee members found little hard evidence of an active conspiracy among arms makers, yet the panel's reports did little to weaken the popular prejudice against “greedy munitions interests.”

sources.title: Senate investigations (list)
quotes: 1934-1936 Special Committee Investigating the Munitions Industry (The Nye Munitions Committee)
Investigation of the manufacturing and sale of munitions and the economic circumstances of U.S. entry into World War I.

sources.publisher: Ruhr-Universität Bochum source collection, reproducing the committee's 1936 report (74th Congress, 2d session)
sources.title: Report of the Special Committee on Investigation of the Munitions Industry: Findings (excerpts)
quotes: the committee finds that the matter of national defense should be above and separated from lobbying and the use of political influence by self-interested groups and that it has not been above or separated from either of them.

there is a record of their active opposition by some to almost all such proposals, of resentment toward them, of contempt for those responsible for them, and of violation of such controls whenever established, and of rich profiting whenever such proposals failed.

changes: Narrowed and sourced. The Senate's own history says the committee 'found little hard evidence of an active conspiracy', so the body now says so. 'Lobbied for military buildup' -> what the report found: arms makers opposed disarmament proposals and profited when they failed, and defense policy was not kept separate from their lobbying. Bankers are represented by J. P. Morgan Jr. among the witnesses. Added URLs.
notes: The 'court' tag here means a congressional investigation. The Bochum page is a German university's source collection reproducing the report's findings. Its citation is to the official Senate report. The Senate's 'Merchants of Death' page carries no date.

title: “War is a racket”
body: Smedley Butler, a retired Marine major general with two Medals of Honor, wrote in 1935 that during his 33 years in the Marine Corps he had spent most of his time being “a high-class muscle man for Big Business, for Wall Street and for the bankers.”
src_label: Butler, Common Sense magazine (Nov 1935); Naval History and Heritage Command

sources.publisher: Montclair State University (course reading by Prof. Grover Furr, transcribing Common Sense)
sources.title: Smedley D. Butler, "America's Armed Forces: 2. 'In Time of Peace': The Army", Common Sense, Vol. 4, No. 11 (November 1935), pp. 8–12
quotes: [Originally published in Common Sense, Vol. 4, No. 11 (November, 1935), pp. 8-12]
I spent 33 years and 4 months In active service as a member of our country's most agile military force -- the Marine Corps.
And during that period I spent most of my time being a high-class muscle man for Big Business, for Wall Street and for the bankers.

sources.publisher: Naval History and Heritage Command (U.S. Navy)
sources.title: Butler, Smedley D.
quotes: For his "distinguished conduct in battle" on this occasion, Butler was awarded the Medal of Honor.
For his "bravery and forceful leadership," Butler was awarded his second Medal of Honor.
In November, Butler was promoted to Major General.
After two years at Quantico, he retired in October 1931 and was placed on the retired list.

changes: No factual change. 'Spent his career as' -> 'spent most of his time being', his own words, with the 33 years. Replaced Wikipedia with a transcription of the Common Sense article and the Navy's biography.
notes: The transcription is a university-hosted course reading, not a scan of the magazine. It notes that the editor omitted some sections, but the quoted sentence is in the transcribed text. The Federation of American Scientists prints a near-identical passage as 'an excerpt from a speech delivered in 1933' ('a high class muscle- man for Big Business, for Wall Street and for the Bankers'). The words may first have been spoken in 1933 and printed in 1935. The Marine Corps University biography (usmcu.edu) was blocked to scripted fetches.

title: Iran: a coup after oil was nationalized
body: After Iran nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company (later BP), the CIA, with British help, engineered a coup against Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq. Its efforts included planting “damaging innuendo in local Iranian media.” A CIA history released in 2013 says the coup was carried out “under CIA direction.”
src_label: Declassified CIA history, The Battle for Iran (released 2013); National Security Archive EBB 435; The Guardian (Aug 2013)

sources.publisher: National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 435 (ed. Malcolm Byrne)
sources.title: CIA Confirms Role in 1953 Iran Coup
quotes: today's posting includes what is believed to be the CIA's first formal acknowledgement that the agency helped to plan and execute the coup.
This appears to be an example of CIA propaganda aimed at undermining Mosaddeq's public standing, presumably prepared during Summer 1953.
It certainly fits the pattern of what Donald Wilber and others after him have described about the nature of the CIA's efforts to plant damaging innuendo in local Iranian media.

sources.publisher: The Guardian (Saeed Kamali Dehghan and Richard Norton-Taylor)
sources.title: CIA admits role in 1953 Iranian coup
quotes: The documents, published on the archive's website under freedom of information laws, describe in detail how the US – with British help – engineered the coup, codenamed TPAJAX by the CIA and Operation Boot by Britain's MI6.
after the Iranian leader nationalised the British Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, latterly known as BP.

changes: No factual change. 'Planted press stories' now quotes the National Security Archive's description. 'Formally acknowledged in 2013' -> a CIA history released in 2013, since the archive calls it what is 'believed to be' the first formal acknowledgement. Fixed the URL: the old nsarchive.gwu.edu/media/... link redirects to the Guardian article. Both are now cited directly.
notes: The CIA history (The Battle for Iran) dates from the mid-1970s. A heavily excised version came out in 1981, and the TPAJAX references were released in 2013. The planted media items in the archive are Iranian-press propaganda, not US press.

title: Guatemala: a fruit company’s PR war
body: Guatemala’s land reform confiscated a quarter of a million acres of United Fruit land in 1953. The CIA’s own history says the company’s PR adviser, Edward Bernays, “laid down a PR barrage” that sent US reporters to cover “Communist activities in Guatemala.” President Eisenhower authorized the CIA operation that ended with elected president Jacobo Árbenz resigning in June 1954.
src_label: CIA History Staff, Operation PBSUCCESS (Cullather, 1994; declassified 1997); National Security Archive EBB 4

sources.publisher: National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 4 (eds. Kate Doyle and Peter Kornbluh)
sources.title: CIA and Assassinations: The Guatemala 1954 Documents
quotes: Arbenz was elected President of Guatemala in 1950
PBSUCCESS, authorized by President Eisenhower in August 1953,
after the CIA installed Castillo Armas in power
up until the day Arbenz resigned on June 27, 1954

changes: No factual change. Quoted the CIA history's own description of Bernays's campaign. Added the size of the land confiscation (1953) without claiming which came first. 'The CIA then backed a coup' -> Eisenhower authorized the CIA operation, which ended with Arbenz's resignation (June 27, 1954) and Castillo Armas installed. Added URLs (the item had none).
notes: The CIA reading-room PDF did not load for a scripted fetch, so I checked the quotes against the Internet Archive's OCR of the same CIA document (DOC_0000134974). The CIA's sentence says Bernays sent correspondents to report on 'Communist activities'. A nearby OCR-garbled passage says he campaigned to persuade Congress and officials that attacks on the company were proof of Communist complicity. 'Painting the government as communist' is a fair summary, and the body now quotes instead. Bitter Fruit (Schlesinger & Kinzer) is cited inside the CIA history but was not read here.

title: Gulf of Tonkin: an attack that didn’t happen
body: President Johnson cited a reported second North Vietnamese attack on US ships, on August 4, 1964, to back his request for a congressional resolution giving the White House freedom of action in Vietnam. An NSA historian’s study, declassified in 2005, concluded that the second attack did not occur.
src_label: Hanyok, NSA Cryptologic Quarterly, declassified 2005; National Security Archive

sources.publisher: National Security Archive, Electronic Briefing Book No. 132 (update)
sources.title: Tonkin Gulf Intelligence "Skewed" According to Official History and Intercepts
quotes: Included in the release is a controversial article by Agency historian Robert J. Hanyok on SIGINT and the Tonkin Gulf which confirms what historians have long argued: that there was no second attack on U.S. ships in Tonkin on August 4, 1964.

President Johnson and Secretary of Defense McNamara treated Agency SIGINT reports as vital evidence of a second attack and used this claim to support retaliatory air strikes and to buttress the administration's request for a Congressional resolution that would give the White House freedom of action in Vietnam.
"The overwhelming body of reports, if used, would have told the story that no attack occurred."

changes: No factual change. Added the date and the White House's use of the claim, as the archive describes it.
notes: Hanyok's article first appeared in NSA's classified Cryptologic Quarterly in early 2001 and was declassified on December 1, 2005, with over 140 other documents. The NSA's own release page was not fetched. The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution itself (Aug 7, 1964) is not quoted here, but the archive page covers the resolution request.

title: Nayirah: invented testimony sells a war
body: A 15-year-old girl told the Congressional Human Rights Caucus in October 1990 that she had watched Iraqi soldiers take babies from incubators in Kuwait and leave them to die. She was the daughter of Kuwait’s ambassador to the US, presented by Hill & Knowlton, the PR firm the Kuwaiti-financed group Citizens for a Free Kuwait had hired for a roughly $10 million campaign for war. ABC found the story almost certainly false, and Amnesty International later retracted its support for it.
src_label: MacArthur, New York Times op-ed (Jan 6, 1992); Middle East Report (1992)

sources.publisher: The New York Times (John R. MacArthur, op-ed)
sources.title: Remember Nayirah, Witness for Kuwait?
quotes: the most sensational one -- that Iraqi soldiers removed hundreds of Kuwaiti babies from incubators and left them to die on hospital floors -- was shown to be almost certainly false by an ABC reporter, John Martin, in March 1991
(Amnesty International later retracted its support of the story.)

the 15-year-old Kuwaiti girl who shocked the Congressional Human Rights Caucus on Oct. 10, 1990, when she tearfully asserted that she had watched 15 infants being taken from incubators in Al-Adan Hospital in Kuwait City by Iraqi soldiers who "left the babies on the cold floor to die."
Nayirah, her real name, is the daughter of the Kuwaiti Ambassador to the U.S., Saud Nasir al-Sabah.
Hill and Knowlton, the public relations firm hired by Citizens for a Free Kuwait, the Kuwaiti-financed group that lobbied Congress for military intervention.
Mr. Hymel presented the witnesses, including Nayirah.

sources.title: The News Industry
quotes: ran a $10 million advertising campaign to build public support for the US war against Iraq.
They coached Nayirah and other purportedly credible “eyewitnesses” to Iraqi atrocities, and made sure their accounts reached every possible media outlet.

changes: 'Paid about $10.8 million' -> 'a roughly $10 million campaign': no source I could read gives $10.8 million, and published figures range from $10 million to $11.9 million. 'Never substantiated' -> ABC's finding as the NYT reports it ('almost certainly false'). Kept 'coached', which rests on MERIP. Added her age and the date. Status documented -> reported, since the key facts come from journalism. Replaced Wikipedia.
notes: nytimes.com cannot be fetched here, so I read the op-ed from a Wayback Machine capture of its nytimes.com URL. The MERIP piece is a column under a pen name ('Al Miskin'). It cites Middle East Watch's February 6, 1992 report 'Kuwait's Stolen Incubators', which would be a stronger source for the falsity finding if it can be found. MacArthur's book Second Front and the ABC 20/20 segment were not read. Hill & Knowlton denied wrongdoing. If the editor wants 'coached' on firmer ground, the CBC/ABC 1992 broadcasts are the usual citation.

title: Iraq’s missing weapons and the press that repeated them
body: A presidential commission concluded that US intelligence was “dead wrong in almost all of its pre-war judgments about Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction.” The New York Times later published an editors’ note saying it had found “a number of instances of coverage that was not as rigorous as it should have been.”
src_label: New York Times, “From the Editors” (May 26, 2004); Commission on the Intelligence Capabilities of the US Regarding WMD (Mar 2005)

sources.title: FROM THE EDITORS; The Times and Iraq
quotes: But we have found a number of instances of coverage that was not as rigorous as it should have been.
Administration officials now acknowledge that they sometimes fell for misinformation from these exile sources. So did many news organizations -- in particular, this one.

sources.publisher: Commission on the Intelligence Capabilities of the United States Regarding Weapons of Mass Destruction (U.S. Government Publishing Office)
sources.title: Report to the President of the United States
quotes: We conclude that the Intelligence Community was dead wrong in almost all of its pre-war judgments about Iraq's weapons of mass destruction. This was a major intelligence failure.

changes: No factual change. 'Claims proved false' is now sourced to the WMD Commission's finding, and the Times quote is given in its full sentence. Added URLs.
notes: nytimes.com cannot be fetched here, so I read the editors' note from a Wayback Machine capture of its nytimes.com URL. CPI's 'False Pretenses' (WAR_STATS-1) also says 'It is now beyond dispute that Iraq did not possess any weapons of mass destruction'.

title: Paid to praise a law
body: The Department of Education, through the PR firm Ketchum, paid commentator Armstrong Williams’s company $186,000 for him to comment regularly on the No Child Left Behind Act on his shows, and took no steps to tell his audiences who was paying. The Government Accountability Office ruled it illegal “covert propaganda.”
src_label: GAO decision B-305368 (Sept 30, 2005)

sources.title: B-305368, Department of Education--Contract to Obtain Services of Armstrong Williams
quotes: The Department of Education contracted to obtain commentary on the No Child Left Behind Act by Mr. Armstrong Williams, but took no steps to assure that its role in sponsoring that commentary was disclosed to the targeted audiences. This constituted covert propaganda in violation of the fiscal year 2004 publicity or propaganda prohibition
The Department told us that it has paid Ketchum a total of $188,543.48 for Task Order Nos. 9 and 16. Of that amount, $186,000 covered amounts that Ketchum paid GWG.

notes: GWG is the Graham Williams Group, Williams's company. The press at the time reported a $240,000 contract. The GAO's figure for money actually paid to his firm is $186,000, which is what the body uses. The GAO also found an Antideficiency Act violation. gao.gov blocks scripted fetches, so I read the decision in a browser and copied the quotes from the page text.

title: “In Washington, I’m Karen Ryan reporting”
body: The Medicare agency paid for ready-made TV news segments about the new Medicare drug law, narrated by “Karen Ryan” and made by a firm hired by its PR contractor Ketchum, that local stations aired without saying the government made them. The GAO ruled that the unattributed story packages broke the ban on federal publicity or propaganda.
src_label: GAO decision B-302710 (May 19, 2004)

sources.title: B-302710, Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services--Video News Releases
quotes: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services's (CMS) use of appropriated funds to pay for the production and distribution of story packages that were not attributed to CMS violated the restriction on using appropriated funds for publicity or propaganda purposes
Although the English story packages contain several of the same B-roll video clips and the same narrator, identified as Karen Ryan, the contents of the two story packages vary.
In Washington, I'm Karen Ryan reporting.
Ketchum hired Home Front Communications (HFC) to create the VNR materials.
CMS provided us a list of television stations that aired at least some portion of the VNRs between January 22, 2004, and February 12, 2004.

notes: The GAO quotes the sign-off with quotation marks, and they drop out of the page's text layer. The words are as quoted. 'Aired without saying the government made them' rests on the GAO's 'story packages that were not attributed to CMS'. The GAO does not list the stations here, beyond naming WBRZ Baton Rouge as one that aired it. gao.gov blocks scripted fetches, so I read the decision in a browser and copied the quotes from the page text.

title: A propaganda office for the Great War
body: Executive Order 2594 of April 13, 1917 created the Committee on Public Information, chaired by George Creel. The National Archives lists its jobs as releasing government news during World War I, sustaining morale and administering “voluntary press censorship.” Its files include “propaganda records” and the work of the “four minute men.”
src_label: National Archives, Records of the Committee on Public Information (Record Group 63)

sources.publisher: U.S. National Archives and Records Administration
sources.title: Records of the Committee on Public Information (Record Group 63)
quotes: Established: As an independent agency by EO 2594, April 13, 1917. Consisted of George Creel (Chairman) and Secretaries of State, War, and the Navy as ex officio members.
Functions: Released government news during World War I. Sustained morale. Administered voluntary press censorship.
Propaganda records, 1917-21.

Reports and correspondence relating to the preparation and distribution of information, the use of motion picture film and photographs, the work of the "four minute men," and the war work of women, 1917-19.

notes: This fills a gap: the WAR section has no case about the US government's own wartime propaganda machinery before the Cold War. NARA also names Carl Byoir as an associate chairman. Byoir and Edward Bernays (WAR-3) both went on to found PR firms, a link worth a separate source if the editor wants it. Counts of the Four Minute Men (often given as 75,000) were not sourced here. archives.gov blocks scripted fetches, so I read the page in a browser and copied the quotes from the page text.

t: an estimated yearly spend by US employers on consultants to fight unionization, likely an undercount.
src_label: Economic Policy Institute (March 2023)

sources.title: Employers spend more than $400 million per year on ‘union-avoidance’ consultants to bolster their union-busting efforts (fact sheet; McNicholas, Poydock, Sanders, Zipperer)
quotes: EPI estimates employers spend $433 million per year on union-avoidance consultants.
This estimate is just a drop in the bucket because there is not enough data to reveal the true scope of what employers spend.
To arrive at the $433 million figure, we take the $338 million dollar estimate from McNicholas et al. 2019, which covered the four-year period

notes: The fact sheet's HTML page (epi.org/publication/union-avoidance/) sits behind a Cloudflare check for automated fetches; the quotes come from EPI's own PDF of the same fact sheet, which is a stable link to use instead. The $433M is EPI's earlier 2014-2017 estimate ($338M) restated in 2023 dollars, not a new count.

t: paid by Amazon to anti-union consultants in 2022 alone, roughly triple the year before.
src_label: US Department of Labor filings; HuffPost (March 2023)

sources.title: Amazon Spent $14 Million On Anti-Union Consultants In 2022 (Dave Jamieson)
quotes: Amazon spent more than $14.2 million last year on outside consultants whose job was to convince workers not to unionize, according to new disclosures filed Friday with the Labor Department.
Amazon spent $4.3 million on anti-union consultants in 2021, HuffPost reported.

notes: $14.2M / $4.3M = 3.3x, so 'more than triple' would be equally accurate. The figure comes from Amazon's disclosures to the Labor Department as reported by HuffPost; the filing itself was not fetched.

title: The Powell Memo
body: Corporate lawyer Lewis Powell, two months before his Supreme Court nomination, sent the US Chamber of Commerce a confidential memo urging business to organize and fund a long-range campaign on campuses, in the media, in the courts and in politics. It is often called the blueprint for the think tanks and business law groups that followed; the clearest direct line runs to the Pacific Legal Foundation (1973), and some writers argue its influence is overstated.
src_label: Powell, “Attack on American Free Enterprise System” (Aug 23, 1971), Washington and Lee University School of Law; Schmitt, “The Legend of the Powell Memo,” The American Prospect (2005)

sources.publisher: Washington and Lee University School of Law, Powell Archives
sources.title: Powell Memorandum: Attack On American Free Enterprise System
quotes: On August 23, 1971, less than two months before he was nominated to serve as an Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States, Lewis F. Powell, Jr. mailed a confidential memorandum to his friend Eugene B. Sydnor, Jr., Chair of the Education Committee of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.
The memo was titled Attack On American Free Enterprise System and outlined ways in which business should defend and counter attack against a "broad attack" from "disquieting voices."

sources.publisher: Reclaim Democracy (full transcription of the memo)
sources.title: Powell Memo (text of the Aug. 23, 1971 memorandum)
quotes: Strength lies in organization, in careful long-range planning and implementation, in consistency of action over an indefinite period of years, in the scale of financing available only through joint effort, and in the political power available only through united action and national organizations.
The Chamber should consider establishing a staff of highly qualified scholars in the social sciences who do believe in the system.
The national television networks should be monitored in the same way that textbooks should be kept under constant surveillance.
This is a vast area of opportunity for the Chamber, if it is willing to undertake the role of spokesman for American business and if, in turn, business is willing to provide the funds.
As unwelcome as it may be to the Chamber, it should consider assuming a broader and more vigorous role in the political arena.

sources.title: The Legend of the Powell Memo (Mark Schmitt)
quotes: Today, though, the Powell Memo is routinely invoked as the blueprint for virtually all of the conservative intellectual infrastructure built in the 1970s and 1980s
and then to the 1973 establishment of the Pacific Legal Foundation
Other than the Pacific Legal Foundation and the tenuous Coors-Heritage connection, it’s hard to find much evidence that the memo served as a direct blueprint for the institutions that followed.

changes: Replaced 'Think tanks and legal groups followed' with a sourced, hedged version: the memo's influence on later think tanks is widely asserted but contested (Schmitt finds a documented line only to the Pacific Legal Foundation). Added that the memo went to the Chamber via its education committee chair and was confidential.
notes: The original typescript PDF on scholarlycommons.law.wlu.edu is behind a Cloudflare check for automated fetches, so memo quotes are taken from Reclaim Democracy's transcription (an advocacy site, but a verbatim copy of the document). An editor can confirm them against the W&L scan by hand. W&L's landing page itself was fetched and quoted.

title: Big Tobacco’s fake smokers’ movement
body: PR firm Burson-Marsteller created the National Smokers Alliance for Philip Morris in 1993 to look like a grassroots smokers’ rights group, with a Burson-Marsteller vice president as its president. Philip Morris supplied its start-up grant, and a peer-reviewed study calls it a front group funded by the tobacco industry.
src_label: Tobacco Tactics, University of Bath; Givel, Journal of Health Communication (2007); NSA fact sheet, UCSF Industry Documents Library

sources.title: Astroturfing
quotes: The following year, in 1993, this team created the National Smokers Alliance on behalf of Philip Morris.
There was also an overlap of staff: The Alliance’s president was the vice president of Burson-Marsteller, and other Burson-Marsteller executives were actively involved in the organisation.
However, the names of the NSA’s corporate funders and organisers were kept off the group’s materials, according to PR Watch.

sources.title: Consent and counter-mobilization: the case of the national smokers alliance (Michael Givel)
quotes: In 1993, the tobacco industry counter-mobilized through the National Smokers Alliance (NSA), a public relations created front group funded by the tobacco industry, which operated nationally from 1994 to 1999

changes: Removed '$42 million raised in its first four years': it is not on the cited Tobacco Tactics page. The only trace found was a 1990s wire story (reportedly citing California Attorney General filings) in a newspaper archive behind a bot wall, so it could not be read or quoted. Replaced it with the founding grant and staff overlap, which the sources state.
notes: If the editor wants the dollar figure back, it needs the original news story or the California AG charity filings in hand. Date of the UCSF document is approximate (the fact sheet describes the group as newly organizing).

title: Oil industry “Energy Citizens” rallies
body: The American Petroleum Institute organized rallies against climate legislation, presented as citizen events. An email from API’s president, leaked by Greenpeace, asked member companies to recruit employees, retirees, vendors and contractors.
src_label: API email to members, published by Greenpeace (Aug 12, 2009); DeSmog (Aug 13, 2009)

sources.publisher: Greenpeace USA (letter to API, with the leaked API email attached)
sources.title: Letter from Phil Radford to Jack Gerard, with copy of email from American Petroleum Institute to its membership
quotes: API is coordinating a series of "Energy Citizen" rallies in about 20 states across the country during the last two weeks of Congress's August recess.

The objective of these rallies is to put a human face on the impacts of unsound energy policy and to aim a loud message at those states' U.S. Senators to avoid the mistakes embodied in the House climate bill
In addition, please include all vendors, suppliers, contractors, retirees and others who have an interest in our success.
we don't want critics to know our game plan.

changes: Body unchanged. Source label: The Guardian (Aug 2009) was not checked (our fetch tools cannot reach theguardian.com), so it is replaced by the leaked email itself as published with Greenpeace's letter.
notes: The email asks member CEOs for each facility manager's 'commitment to provide significant attendance' and to include vendors, suppliers, contractors and retirees; 'employees' is DeSmog's summary of the facility-attendance ask.

title: Billionaire fuel for the Tea Party
body: Groups funded by Charles and David Koch, including Americans for Prosperity, provided money, training and organization to the Tea Party movement. The Kochs denied funding the Tea Party directly.
src_label: Mayer, “Covert Operations,” The New Yorker (2010)

sources.title: Covert Operations (Jane Mayer)
quotes: the advocacy wing of the Americans for Prosperity Foundation—an organization that David Koch started, in 2004—held a different kind of gathering.

She explained that the role of Americans for Prosperity was to help “educate” Tea Party activists on policy details, and to give them “next-step training” after their rallies, so that their political energy could be channelled “more effectively.”
By giving money to “educate,” fund, and organize Tea Party protesters, they have helped turn their private agenda into a mass movement.
“No funding has been provided by Koch companies, the Koch foundations, or Charles Koch or David Koch specifically to support the tea parties.”

changes: Added the URL.
notes: Posted online Aug 23, 2010; print issue dated Aug 30, 2010.

title: Foreign trolls stage both sides of a protest
body: Russia’s Internet Research Agency used a fake “Heart of Texas” Facebook page to promote a “Stop Islamization of Texas” protest at a Houston Islamic center on May 21, 2016, and a second fake page to promote a counter-rally at the same place and time. The two crowds faced off; the ads cost about $200.
src_label: Senate Intelligence Committee report, Vol. 2 (2019); NPR (Nov 2017)

sources.publisher: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
sources.title: Russian Active Measures Campaigns and Interference in the 2016 U.S. Election, Volume 2: Russia's Use of Social Media
quotes: IRA influence operatives used the Facebook page, "Heart of Texas" to promote a protest in opposition to Islam, to occur in front of the Islamic Da'wah Center in Houston, Texas.

"Heart of Texas," which eventually attracted over 250,000 followers, used targeted advertisements to implore its supporters to attend a "Stop Islamization of Texas" event, slated for noon, May 21, 2016.
to promote a second event, to be held at the same time, at exactly the same Islamic Da'wah Center in Houston.

sources.title: How Russia Used Facebook To Organize 2 Sets Of Protesters (Ryan Lucas)
quotes: In May of last year, two groups of demonstrators faced off outside the Islamic Center in Houston Texas.
Russian operatives had established both Facebook groups.
The price tag on all this - it set Russia back a grand total of around $200.

changes: 'organized a Houston protest against a mosque' -> 'promote a Stop Islamization of Texas protest at a Houston Islamic center': the Senate report says the IRA promoted the event, outside the Islamic Da'wah Center, through targeted ads. Added the date, the page names, the face-off and the ~$200 cost.
notes: The Senate report names the second page "United Muslims for America" in one place and NPR calls it "United Muslims of America"; the body avoids the name.

title: Culture war as a substitute for wages
body: Writer Thomas Frank argued that political campaigns rally working-class voters around cultural grievances while delivering economic policies that favor the wealthy.
src_label: Frank, What’s the Matter with Kansas? (2004)

sources.publisher: Metropolitan Books / Macmillan (excerpt of the introduction)
sources.title: What's the Matter with Kansas? How Conservatives Won the Heart of America (Thomas Frank)
quotes: While earlier forms of conservatism emphasized fiscal sobriety, the backlash mobilizes voters with explosive social issues—summoning public outrage over everything from busing to un-Christian art—which it then marries to pro-business economic policies.
Cultural anger is marshaled to achieve economic ends.
Vote to stop abortion; receive a rollback in capital gains taxes.

changes: Added the URL (publisher's excerpt of Frank's introduction, in his own words).
notes: The Macmillan listing is the paperback with a new afterword; the book first appeared in 2004.

title: “Right to work” was born in a racist, “Christian” front group
body: Texas lobbyist Vance Muse’s Christian American Association, which raised money from wealthy Southern planters and industrialists, led the 1944 campaign that made Arkansas, with Florida, one of the first two states to pass a “right to work” law, selling it with racist and antisemitic propaganda.
src_label: Pierce, “The Origins of Right-to-Work,” LAWCHA (2017)

sources.title: The Origins of Right-to-Work: Vance Muse, Anti-Semitism, and the Maintenance of Jim Crow Labor Relations (Michael Pierce)
quotes: In 1936, on the heels of the Southern Committee’s failure to deny Roosevelt’s nomination, Muse incorporated the Christian American Association to continue the fight against the New Deal, offering up a toxic mix of anti-Semitism, racism, anti-Communism, and anti-unionism.
The Christian Americans solicited wealthy southern planters and industrialists for funds

The Arkansas Farm Bureau Federation and allied industrialists were so pleased with the Christian American Association’s success in passing the anti-strike measure that they agreed to underwrite a campaign in 1944 to secure a Right-to-Work amendment for the Arkansas constitution.
While Muse and the Christian Americans consulted with the campaigns in California and Florida, they led the one in Arkansas.
In November 1944, Arkansas and Florida became the first states to enact Right-to-Work laws (California voters rejected the measure).

changes: Narrowed 'pushed the first right to work laws (Arkansas and Florida, 1944)': Pierce says Muse's group led the Arkansas campaign and only consulted on Florida's. 'Funded by' became 'raised money from', which is how Pierce puts it. Year label 1936-40s -> 1936-44 (incorporation to the 1944 votes).
notes: Dixon, Journal of Policy History (2007) ("Limiting Labor", doi 10.1353/jph.2007.0015) exists, but its text was not read, so it is dropped from the label. Michael Pierce is a historian at the University of Arkansas. A 1907 aside worth knowing: Rauschenbusch already wrote that the cry of 'the right to work' had been 'raised mainly by the employers' (see RECLAIM-1).

title: Prayer breakfasts born from anti-union organizing
body: In April 1935, Norwegian-born preacher Abraham Vereide gathered Seattle business executives into weekly prayer breakfasts; journalist Jeff Sharlet, working from the group’s own archive, writes that they prayed to “crush the radical unions.” His network, the Fellowship (or “the Family”), established the National Prayer Breakfast in 1953.
src_label: Sharlet, “Jesus Plus Nothing,” Harper’s (March 2003); Pacific Lutheran University Archives

sources.title: Jesus Plus Nothing (Jeff Sharlet)
quotes: Between 1984 and 1992 the Fellowship Foundation consigned 592 boxes—decades of the Family’s letters, sermons, minutes, Christmas cards, travel itineraries, and lists of members—to an archive at the Billy Graham Center of Wheaton College in Illinois.
The Family was founded in April 1935 by Abraham Vereide, a Norwegian immigrant who made his living as a traveling preacher.
They enlisted nineteen business executives in a weekly breakfast meeting and together they prayed, convinced that Jesus alone could redeem Seattle and crush the radical unions.
The Family’s only publicized gathering is the National Prayer Breakfast, which it established in 1953

sources.title: Abraham Vereide (biographical note)
quotes: In 1935, Vereide founded the prayer breakfast movement in the United States.
In 1953, Vereide started the Presidential Prayer Breakfast, later called the National Prayer Breakfast or the International Prayer Breakfast.

changes: 'Methodist minister' -> 'Norwegian-born preacher': no fetched source names his denomination. 'Fighting organized labor among their stated concerns' -> Sharlet's own words ('crush the radical unions'), attributed to him. Added April 1935.
notes: Sharlet's book The Family (2008) expands this article but was not checked here, so the label cites the article. Wheaton's finding aid for the Fellowship Foundation Records (archives.wheaton.edu) sits behind a human check and was not read.

title: Industrialists fund “Freedom Under God”
body: Corporate leaders including Sun Oil president J. Howard Pew and GM’s Alfred Sloan, along with the heads of the US Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers, bankrolled minister James Fifield’s Spiritual Mobilization, which recruited clergy to preach that the New Deal was “pagan stateism” under the slogan “Freedom Under God.” Historian Kevin Kruse traces how that pairing of faith and free enterprise moved to center stage in the 1950s, when “under God” entered the Pledge (1954) and “In God We Trust” became the national motto (1956).
src_label: Kruse, One Nation Under God (2015), interviewed on NPR’s Fresh Air (March 2015); Eisenhower signing statement (June 14, 1954)

sources.title: How 'One Nation' Didn't Become 'Under God' Until The '50s Religious Revival
quotes: So they argue that the New Deal is not a manifestation of God's will, but rather, a form of pagan stateism and is inherently sinful.
"Spiritual mobilization" is his effort to recruit other ministers to the cause.

His main sponsors are Sun Oil President J. Howard Pew, Alfred Sloan of General Motors, the heads of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the National Association of Manufacturers, they all heavily fund this organization.
He comes up with the phrase that reduces this Christian libertarian ideology down to a catchy slogan and that slogan is "Freedom Under God," as opposed to the slavery of the state.
He says this conflation of Christianity and capitalism moved to center stage in the '50s under Eisenhower's watch.
And in 1956, they move to make it the country's first official national motto.

sources.publisher: The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara
sources.title: Statement by the President Upon Signing Bill To Include the Words "Under God" in the Pledge to the Flag
quotes: Statement by the President Upon Signing Bill To Include the Words "Under God" in the Pledge to the Flag. June 14, 1954

changes: Removed Harvey Firestone: Kruse names Pew, Sloan and the heads of the Chamber and NAM as the main sponsors, not Firestone. Added Fifield's slogan in Kruse's words, and the 1954 Pledge date from Eisenhower's signing statement (the NPR piece only says 'the 1950s'). Year label 1940s-50s -> 1930s-50s (NPR: the campaign ran through the 1930s and '40s).
notes: Firestone may well appear in Kruse's book, but that was not checked; restore him only with a page cite.

title: The religious right’s real starting point
body: Historian Randall Balmer argues the religious right first organized not around abortion but around federal moves to deny tax exemptions to racially segregated Christian schools, with strategist Paul Weyrich using the issue to mobilize preachers like Jerry Falwell.
src_label: Balmer, “The Historian’s Pickaxe” (essay); Bad Faith (2021). Critics dispute this account.

sources.publisher: Andrea Mitchell Center, University of Pennsylvania
sources.title: The Historian's Pickaxe: Uncovering the Racist Origins of the Religious Right (Randall Balmer)
quotes: Weyrich forcefully disputed that assumption, recounting that ever since Barry Goldwater's run for the presidency in 1964, he had been trying to enlist evangelicals in conservative political causes, but it was the tax exemption for religious schools that finally caught the attention of evangelical leaders.
Green v. Connally served as the catalyst, not Roe v. Wade.
prompted preachers like Jerry Falwell to mobilize against him.

sources.title: In Good Faith
quotes: In his latest book, Bad Faith: Race and the Rise of the Religious Right (2021), Balmer calls the widely accepted view that the 1973 Roe v. Wade decision drove evangelicals into the political arena a myth.
Rather, he argues, what galvanized religious right leaders was the threat that their racially discriminatory schools would lose their tax-exempt status.

sources.publisher: The Gospel Coalition (guest post by attorney Jonathan Whitehead)
sources.title: Fact-Checking Randall Balmer’s Urban Legend on the Real Origin of the Religious Right
quotes: So the core allegations of the Balmer story are wrong.

changes: 'Paul Weyrich recruiting Jerry Falwell' -> Weyrich used the schools issue to mobilize preachers like Falwell, which is how Balmer puts it. 'IRS stripping tax exemptions' -> 'federal moves to deny tax exemptions' (Balmer's catalyst is the 1971 Green v. Connally ruling, then IRS actions). Year 1979 -> 1971-79. 'Some historians dispute' -> 'Critics dispute': the critique found is by an attorney, not a historian.
notes: Balmer's Politico Magazine piece (May 2014) could not be fetched (politico.com is blocked to our tools), so it is dropped from the label in favour of his essay hosted by UPenn, which makes the same argument in his own words. Wording in the essay that the PDF splits across a line ('tax-exempt') was avoided in quotes.

title: Climate action as a “false religion”
body: The Cornwall Alliance, an evangelical group that co-sponsored the Heartland Institute’s 2009 conference on climate change and shares a fundraising firm with the group CFACT, released “Resisting the Green Dragon,” a 12-part DVD series casting environmentalism as a rival faith with “its own doctrines of God, creation, humanity, sin, and salvation.”
src_label: Cornwall Alliance press release, via Mother Jones (Dec 2010); DeSmog

sources.title: Beware the Treehuggers! (Kate Sheppard)
quotes: Just in time for the holidays, a coalition of Christian conservative groups has issued an “explosive new 12-part DVD series” detailing the dangers of environmentalism.
“Today’s environmentalism isn’t a neutral set of ideas that can be tacked onto the Christian faith without theological compromise,” Beisner said.
“Instead, it promotes its own worldview and its own doctrines of God, creation, humanity, sin, and salvation. And those doctrines aren’t Biblical.”

sources.title: Cornwall Alliance for the Stewardship of Creation (profile)
quotes: The DVD series portrays the entire green movement as a “false religion,” and part of a conspiracy to create a “global government.”
The Cornwall Alliance was a co-sponsor of the Heartland Institute’s 2009 International Conference on Climate Change.

changes: Replaced 'whose leaders have worked with fossil-funded climate-skeptic groups such as CFACT and the Heartland Institute' with the two ties the sources document (co-sponsoring Heartland's 2009 conference; a shared fundraising firm with CFACT). 'Fossil-funded' was dropped because no fetched source states the funding of those two groups. Added Beisner's own words.
notes: Cornwall Alliance's own site returned 403 to our fetch; its press release is quoted through Mother Jones. Cornwall denies any relationship with CFACT, so if the editor shortens the body, keep that hedge in mind. Restoring 'fossil-funded' would need a separate source for Heartland's and CFACT's industry funding.

title: Televangelists’ jets and mansions
body: A Senate Finance Committee inquiry launched by Sen. Chuck Grassley in 2007 examined six TV ministries over high salaries, private jets, luxury cars and homes. Four would not fully cooperate. It ended in 2011 with no penalties, and Grassley asked an evangelical accountability group to study “self-reform.”
src_label: Senate Finance Committee staff review (Jan 6, 2011); Christianity Today; Religion News Service via The Christian Century (2011)

sources.title: Review of Media-Based Ministries (staff memo to Senator Grassley)
quotes: The other four either did not provide a response or provided incomplete responses.

Charitable organizations are frequently criticized for the compensation packages they provide to their officers, directors, trustees and key employees, especially when the package includes luxury vehicles and private jets.
The six media-based ministries were also subject to these criticisms and our reviews of each confirm that such criticisms are warranted.
The value of the houses owned by the churches reviewed by the Committee dwarf that of the house provided to Jim Bakker when he was head of PTL.

sources.title: Grassley Investigation Ends with No Penalty for Televangelists (Sarah Pulliam Bailey)
quotes: Sen. Chuck Grassley's investigation of televangelists finished with no penalties for the pastors who did not cooperate and found no definitive instances of wrongdoing, the Associated Press reports.
Grassley (R-Iowa), who launched the investigation in 2007, released the report at the end of his tenure as the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee.

sources.title: Senator ends probe of ministries, calls for ‘self-reform’ (Adelle M. Banks)
quotes: Sen. Charles Grassley of Iowa, having concluded a three-year probe into alleged lavish spending at six major broadcast ministries, has asked a prominent evangelical group to study ways to spur "self-reform" among religious groups.
The senator asked the Evangelical Council on Financial Accountability to conduct a formal study of issues raised by his staff

changes: 'Six prosperity-gospel ministries' -> 'six TV ministries': none of the sources uses the prosperity-gospel label (they say media-based, broadcast or televangelist). 'Referring reforms to an evangelical self-regulation body' -> Grassley asked the Evangelical Council for Financial Accountability to study self-reform. Added the 2007 start and that four would not fully cooperate.
notes: Christianity Today says the probe 'found no definitive instances of wrongdoing', while the staff memo says its reviews 'confirm that such criticisms are warranted' about jets and pay. Both are true to their sources; the body avoids claiming wrongdoing was proven. The fetched sources name Benny Hinn, Joyce Meyer, Kenneth Copeland and Creflo Dollar among the six; the other two were not checked here.

title: An employer’s faith limits workers’ benefits
body: In Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, the Supreme Court ruled 5–4 that closely held companies can be exempted from covering contraceptives their owners object to on religious grounds.
src_label: Burwell v. Hobby Lobby, US Supreme Court (2014)

sources.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
sources.title: Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores, Inc., 573 U.S. 682 (2014)
quotes: In these cases, the owners of three closely held for-profit corporations have sincere Christian beliefs that life begins at conception and that it would violate their religion to facilitate access to contraceptive drugs or devices that operate after that point.
Held: As applied to closely held corporations, the HHS regulations imposing the contraceptive mandate violate RFRA.
Alito, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which Roberts, C. J., and Scalia, Kennedy, and Thomas, JJ., joined.
Ginsburg, J., filed a dissenting opinion, in which Sotomayor, J., joined, and in which Breyer and Kagan, JJ., joined as to all but Part III–C–1.

changes: Added the URL.
notes: 5-4 = Alito, Roberts, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas against Ginsburg, Sotomayor, Breyer, Kagan. The ruling was under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, not the Constitution.

title: Religious employers exempt from discrimination suits
body: In Our Lady of Guadalupe v. Morrissey-Berru, the Supreme Court extended the “ministerial exception,” barring religious-school teachers who teach the faith from suing over age or disability discrimination.
src_label: Our Lady of Guadalupe School v. Morrissey-Berru, US Supreme Court (2020)

sources.publisher: Supreme Court of the United States
sources.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe School v. Morrissey-Berru, 591 U.S. ___ (2020) (slip opinion)
quotes: Morrissey-Berru claimed that OLG had demoted her and had failed to renew her contract in order to replace her with a younger teacher in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967.
Biel alleged that St. James discharged her because she had requested a leave of absence to obtain breast cancer treatment.
What matters, at bottom, is what an employee does.

changes: Swapped the law-firm URL for the Court's own slip opinion as the main source (the law-firm summary is kept for the 'disability' wording and the 7-2 vote).
notes: The vote was 7-2 (Sotomayor and Ginsburg dissenting); the editor may want it in the body to match FAITH-6. The opinion describes Biel's claim (fired after asking for leave for breast-cancer treatment) without naming the statute in the passages quoted; Holland & Knight states it was a disability claim.

title: Foreign trolls pose as Christians
body: Russia’s Internet Research Agency ran pages like “Army of Jesus,” with more than 216,000 followers, using religious memes to win followers and push election content.
src_label: Senate Intelligence Committee report, Vol. 2 (Oct 2019)

sources.publisher: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence
sources.title: Russian Active Measures Campaigns and Interference in the 2016 U.S. Election, Volume 2: Russia's Use of Social Media
quotes: The tactic of using select payload messages among a large volume of innocuous content to attract and cultivate an online following is reflected in the posts made to the IRA's "Army of Jesus" Facebook page.

The page, which had attracted over 216,000 followers by the time it was taken down by Facebook for violating the platform's terms of service, purported to be devoted to Christian themes and Bible passages.
November 1, 2016: "HILLARY APPROVES REMOVAL OF GOD FROM THE PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE."

notes: The report's example: Bible-verse posts on Oct 26-31 and Nov 2, 2016, around a single Nov 1 'payload' post about Clinton and the Pledge.

title: The Pope backs unions
body: Pope Leo XIII’s encyclical Rerum Novarum defends workers’ right to form unions and earn a just wage.
src_label: Rerum Novarum (1891)

sources.title: Rerum Novarum: Encyclical of Pope Leo XIII on Capital and Labor
quotes: The most important of all are workingmen's unions, for these virtually include all the rest.
For, to enter into a "society" of this kind is the natural right of man

there underlies a dictate of natural justice more imperious and ancient than any bargain between man and man, namely, that wages ought not to be insufficient to support a frugal and well-behaved wage-earner.
Given at St. Peter's in Rome, the fifteenth day of May, 1891

changes: Added the URL.

title: The Social Gospel
body: Baptist minister Walter Rauschenbusch’s Christianity and the Social Crisis calls on churches to take up the social crisis of industrial capitalism and backs the labor movement’s fight to win unions a recognized place in law.
src_label: Rauschenbusch, Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907)

sources.publisher: The American Yawp Reader (Stanford University Press)
sources.title: Walter Rauschenbusch, Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907)
quotes: Walter Rauschenbusch, a Baptist minister and theologian, advocated for a “social gospel.”

It follows that the relation between Christianity and the social crisis is one of the most pressing questions for all intelligent men who realize the power of religion, and most of all for the religious leaders of the people who give direction to the forces of religion.
Whoever uncouples the religious and the social life has not understood Jesus.

changes: 'Calls on churches to fight poverty and exploitation of workers' -> wording that matches what the quoted text says: churches must take up the social crisis, and the labor movement must go on until unions win a recognized position. Same claim, now resting on his own sentences.
notes: The archive.org quotes come from the OCR of the 1907 scan; one word ('position') is split across a line in the OCR and was rejoined for checking. The 'right to work' line ties neatly to FAITH-0.

title: A farmworkers’ pilgrimage
body: César Chávez led striking grape workers on a march to Sacramento framed as a religious pilgrimage, during Lent, under a banner of the Virgin of Guadalupe.
src_label: National Park Service

sources.title: Mobilizing Support for La Causa (series: The Road to Sacramento)
quotes: Cesar Chavez leads marchers across a highway bridge during the 1966 pilgrimage to Sacramento.
After six months of picketing and protest, the Delano Grape strikers remained out of work with no area grower agreeing to a contract.

The march coincided with Lent, drawing on the theme of penance and sacrifice in the Roman Catholic tradition, and was timed to conclude on Easter Sunday, a powerful metaphor for the farmworkers’ aspirations for redemption.
As the farmworkers made their way through the Central Valley, they carried a banner with the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe, the patron saint of Mexico.

title: “All labor has dignity”
body: Martin Luther King Jr. came to Memphis to support striking Black sanitation workers. He was assassinated there weeks later.
src_label: King, speech to Memphis sanitation strikers (March 18, 1968); Stanford King Institute

sources.title: The 50th Anniversary of Martin Luther King, Jr.’s “All Labor Has Dignity”
quotes: Fifty years ago—on March 18, 1968—Martin Luther King, Jr. delivered his speech “All Labor Has Dignity” at Bishop Charles Mason Temple of the Church of God in Christ in Memphis, Tennessee.
But let me say to you tonight, that whenever you are engaged in work that serves humanity and is for the building of humanity, it has dignity, and it has worth.
All labor has dignity.
King was assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee, on April 4, 1968.

sources.publisher: Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University
sources.title: Memphis Sanitation Workers’ Strike
quotes: Eleven days later, frustrated by the city’s response to the latest event in a long pattern of neglect and abuse of its black employees, 1,300 black men from the Memphis Department of Public Works went on strike.
King himself arrived on 18 March to address a crowd of about 25,000—the largest indoor gathering the civil rights movement had ever seen.

changes: Added the Stanford King Institute as the source that the strikers were Black (the Beacon page does not say so).

title: Climate as a moral issue for the poor
body: Pope Francis’s Laudato si’ calls climate change a threat that falls hardest on the poor and criticizes an economy that treats people and nature as disposable.
src_label: Laudato si’ (2015)

sources.title: Laudato si’: Encyclical Letter of the Holy Father Francis on Care for Our Common Home
quotes: Climate change is a global problem with grave implications: environmental, social, economic, political and for the distribution of goods.
Its worst impact will probably be felt by developing countries in coming decades.
Many of the poor live in areas particularly affected by phenomena related to warming
These problems are closely linked to a throwaway culture which affects the excluded just as it quickly reduces things to rubbish.
Given in Rome at Saint Peter’s on 24 May, the Solemnity of Pentecost, in the year 2015

changes: Added the URL.

title: Millions of fake voices for the FCC
body: New York’s attorney general found that the nation’s largest broadband companies secretly funded a campaign to flood the FCC with comments backing its 2017 repeal of net neutrality. The firms they hired fabricated responses, filing more than 8.5 million fake comments in real people’s names; another 9.3 million fakes on the other side came mostly from one college student.
src_label: New York Attorney General, report and press release (May 6, 2021)

sources.publisher: Office of the New York State Attorney General
sources.title: Attorney General James Issues Report Detailing Millions of Fake Comments, Revealing Secret Campaign to Influence FCC’s 2017 Repeal of Net Neutrality Rules
quotes: Through its investigation, the Office of the Attorney General (OAG) found that, in 2017, the nation’s largest broadband companies funded a secret campaign to generate millions of comments to the FCC.
However, nearly every lead generator that was hired to enroll consumers in the campaign, instead, simply fabricated consumers’ responses.
As a result, more than 8.5 million fake comments that impersonated real people were submitted to the FCC, and more than half a million fake letters were sent to Congress.
The OAG also found that the FCC received another 9.3 million fake comments supporting net neutrality that used fictitious identities.
Most of these comments were submitted by a single person — a 19-year old college student using automated software.
In all, the OAG confirmed that nearly 18 million of the more than 22 million comments the FCC received in its 2017 proceeding to repeal net neutrality rules were fake.

notes: A state attorney general's investigation, so tagged court (government inquiry). The release names the practice astroturfing in its own words. The body keeps the pro-net-neutrality fakes in, so the case cannot be read as one-sided.

title: Amazon’s mailbox voids a union vote
body: After workers at Amazon’s Bessemer, Alabama warehouse voted down a union 1,798 to 738, the National Labor Relations Board’s regional director threw out the result and ordered a new election. She found that a postal mailbox Amazon installed at the main employee entrance “essentially highjacked the process.”
src_label: NLRB Region 10 decision (Nov 2021), as reported by the Associated Press / PBS NewsHour

sources.title: Amazon workers in Alabama get a do-over union election (Anne D'Innocenzio)
quotes: The National Labor Relations Board has ordered a new union election for Amazon workers in Bessemer, Alabama based on objections to the first vote that took place in April.
In a 20-page decision, the regional director for the NLRB Lisa Henderson focused much attention on Amazon's installation of a U.S. Postal Service mail box at the main employee entrance
"The employer's flagrant disregard for the board's typical mail-ballot procedure compromised the authority of the board and made a free and fair election impossible," Henderson said in her decision.
"By installing a postal mailbox at the main employee entrance, the employer essentially highjacked the process and gave a strong impression that it controlled the process.
Last time around, 1,798 workers rejected the union and 738 voted in favor of it.

notes: 'Highjacked' is the decision's spelling as quoted by AP. The NLRB Region 10 decision itself was not fetched (the union said it could only be released by the NLRB); nlrb.gov's case search should hold it. The source does not cover the 2022 rerun, so the body stops at the order.

title: A pope defends the right to strike
body: Pope John Paul II’s encyclical Laborem Exercens calls workers’ unions “an indispensable element of social life” and says workers should be assured the right to strike without facing penal sanctions for taking part.
src_label: Laborem Exercens (1981)

sources.title: Laborem Exercens: Encyclical of Pope John Paul II on Human Work
quotes: The experience of history teaches that organizations of this type are an indispensable element of social life, especially in modern industrialized societies.
This method is recognized by Catholic social teaching as legitimate in the proper conditions and within just limits.
In this connection workers should be assured the right to strike, without being subjected to personal penal sanctions for taking part in a strike.
Given at Castel Gandolfo, on the fourteenth day of September, the Feast of the Triumph of the Cross, in the year 1981

notes: The same section warns that a strike 'remains, in a sense, an extreme means' and must not be abused for political purposes; the body does not overstate it.

title: Pentagon’s hidden TV analysts
body: Retired military officers presented on TV as independent analysts were part of a Pentagon campaign to generate favorable coverage of the Iraq war. They echoed administration talking points, and most had ties to military contractors, which was rarely disclosed.
src_label: Barstow, New York Times (Apr 20, 2008); 2009 Pulitzer Prize for Investigative Reporting

sources.title: Behind TV Analysts, Pentagon's Hidden Hand
quotes: Hidden behind that appearance of objectivity, though, is a Pentagon information apparatus that has used those analysts in a campaign to generate favorable news coverage of the administration's wartime performance, an examination by The New York Times has found.

Most of the analysts have ties to military contractors vested in the very war policies they are asked to assess on air. Those business relationships are hardly ever disclosed to the viewers, and sometimes not even to the networks themselves.
In turn, members of this group have echoed administration talking points, sometimes even when they suspected the information was false or inflated.

changes: No factual change. Brought the wording close to the reporting ('campaign to generate favorable news coverage', 'most' had contractor ties), and dated the Pulitzer (2009). Added URLs.
notes: Both pages were read from Wayback Machine captures of their original URLs, because nytimes.com is not fetchable here and pulitzer.org shows a Cloudflare check. Barstow also reports the Pentagon recruited 'more than 75 retired officers'. The Defense Department inspector general reviewed the program in January 2009 and later withdrew that report. Neither is quoted here.
